text_blocks.snippet: Diabetics often feel thirsty due to high blood sugar levels (hyperglycemia) and the resulting increased urination. When blood sugar is high, the kidneys work harder to filter and absorb it. If there's too much sugar, the kidneys pull fluid from tissues to help flush it out through urine, leading to dehydration and thirst.

list.title: High blood sugar (hyperglycemia):
list.snippet: In diabetes, the body either doesn't produce enough insulin or can't properly use the insulin it produces. Insulin helps glucose (sugar) enter cells for energy. Without enough insulin, glucose builds up in the blood.

list.title: Kidneys working overtime:
list.snippet: The kidneys try to remove the excess sugar from the blood by filtering it out through urine.

list.title: Fluid loss through urination:
list.snippet: This process of filtering out excess sugar requires extra water, leading to increased urination and, consequently, dehydration.

list.title: Brain's thirst response:
list.snippet: The body's natural response to dehydration is thirst. The brain signals the need to drink more fluids to replenish what was lost through urination.

list.title: Diabetes insipidus:
list.snippet: While less common, diabetes insipidus can also cause excessive thirst and urination due to the body's inability to regulate fluid balance.
